title: A shared history: perceptron to deep learning
text:
CHAPTER 15  NEUROSCIENCE AND AI

15_01  A SHARED HISTORY: FROM THE PERCEPTRON TO DEEP LEARNING

Throughout this book, each chapter ended by connecting its neuroscience to artificial intelligence. This final chapter turns the relationship around and tells the story from the AI side, as a single narrative, so that the threads scattered across earlier chapters can be seen as one braid. The braid has periods when neuroscience and AI were tightly intertwined, periods when they drifted apart, and a present in which they are again deeply connected, though not always in the ways the founders imagined.

1943: THE LOGICAL NEURON

The story begins, as Chapter 4 described, with Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, whose 1943 paper "A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity" modelled neurons as binary threshold units and showed that networks of them could compute logical functions. Their neuron was a deliberate simplification of the all-or-none spike and synaptic summation described by Adrian and Sherrington. It inspired John von Neumann, whose 1945 draft report on the EDVAC computer described its logic elements by analogy with neurons, and it inspired the cybernetics movement of Norbert Wiener, which treated animals and machines alike as feedback control systems. In the 1940s, the boundaries between neurophysiology, computing and control engineering were thin.

1949: HEBB'S LEARNING RULE

Donald Hebb's 1949 book The Organization of Behavior (Chapter 7) proposed that connections between co-active neurons strengthen and that groups of such neurons form "cell assemblies". McCulloch and Pitts had shown what fixed networks could compute; Hebb suggested how networks could learn. Early computer simulations of Hebbian networks were run in the 1950s, including work by Nathaniel Rochester and colleagues at IBM.

1956 TO 1969: PERCEPTRONS, ADALINE, AND THE FIRST WINTER

The 1956 Dartmouth workshop, organised by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, is usually taken as the founding event of AI as a named field. Its dominant direction for decades would be symbolic: logic, search and rules. But a parallel, brain-inspired direction was launched almost at once.

Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, described the perceptron in a 1958 paper in Psychological Review. It combined McCulloch-Pitts threshold units with a learning rule. For an input vector x, weights w and bias b, the output is

  y = 1 if w . x + b > 0, else 0

and after each example with target t, the weights change by

  w <- w + eta (t - y) x

an error-correcting rule that, unlike pure Hebbian learning, uses a teaching signal. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees that if the classes are linearly separable, the rule finds a separating boundary in finitely many steps. Rosenblatt built the Mark I Perceptron, a hardware machine with an array of photocells and adjustable weights implemented by motor-driven potentiometers, a piece of mechatronics in the literal sense. Press coverage at the time was extravagant in its predictions.

At Stanford, Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff in 1960 introduced ADALINE and the least mean squares (LMS) rule, which minimises squared error on the linear output before thresholding:

  w <- w + eta (t - w . x) x

This is stochastic gradient descent on a linear model. LMS became fundamental in adaptive signal processing, used in echo cancellation and equalisation, and is a direct ancestor of how deep networks are trained.

In 1969 Minsky and Seymour Papert published the book Perceptrons, which analysed rigorously what single-layer perceptrons can and cannot compute. Some functions, famously XOR and properties like connectedness of a figure, cannot be computed by a single layer of threshold units with local receptive fields. Multi-layer networks could compute them, but there was no general method to train them. Together with overstated early claims and funding shifts, the book is commonly associated with a decline in neural network research through the 1970s, although the extent of its causal role is debated by historians. Research continued in smaller groups, for example Kunihiko Fukushima in Japan, Teuvo Kohonen in Finland on self-organising maps, and Stephen Grossberg in the United States on adaptive resonance.

1980: THE NEOCOGNITRON

Fukushima's neocognitron, published in Biological Cybernetics in 1980, is a key link between neuroscience and modern AI. It was explicitly modelled on Hubel and Wiesel's simple and complex cells (Chapter 8): alternating layers of "S-cells" that detect features with local receptive fields and "C-cells" that pool over position to give tolerance to shifts. It was trained with unsupervised, competitive learning rather than backpropagation. Its architecture is essentially the convolutional network with pooling.

1982 TO 1986: HOPFIELD, BOLTZMANN, AND BACKPROPAGATION

John Hopfield's 1982 network (Chapters 9 and 13) used an energy function borrowed from the physics of spin glasses to explain associative memory, attracting physicists to the field. David Ackley, Geoffrey Hinton and Terrence Sejnowski introduced the Boltzmann machine in 1985, a stochastic network with hidden units and a learning rule derived from statistical mechanics that, notably, was local and had a Hebbian form with a sleep-like negative phase.

Backpropagation, the application of the chain rule to compute gradients in multi-layer networks, has a complex history. Related methods were developed in control theory in the 1960s, Seppo Linnainmaa described reverse-mode automatic differentiation in 1970, and Paul Werbos proposed applying it to neural networks in his 1974 Harvard thesis. The 1986 Nature paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", demonstrated convincingly that hidden units trained this way learn useful internal representations, and it brought the method to wide attention. The same year saw the two-volume Parallel Distributed Processing books by Rumelhart, James McClelland and the PDP Research Group, which framed neural networks as models of cognition: "connectionism". For a time, cognitive psychology, neuroscience and machine learning shared a common language.

Chapter 7 discussed why backpropagation seemed biologically implausible: it requires symmetric feedback weights (the weight transport problem), separate forward and backward phases, and precise error signals transmitted backward. Francis Crick wrote in Nature in 1989 that backpropagation was unrealistic as a model of the brain. This tension shaped the relationship between the fields for decades.

1989 TO 2006: CONVOLUTIONAL NETWORKS AND THE SECOND QUIET PERIOD

Yann LeCun and colleagues at Bell Labs combined the neocognitron's architecture with backpropagation, publishing in 1989 a convolutional network for recognising handwritten zip codes, developed into LeNet and deployed to read cheques in the 1990s. Sepp Hochreiter and Jurgen Schmidhuber introduced the long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent network in 1997 to address vanishing gradients in learning long-term dependencies; its gates resemble, loosely, the gating of information flow discussed in neuroscience.

Yet through much of the 1990s and early 2000s, support vector machines, kernel methods and probabilistic graphical models often outperformed neural networks on available datasets and computers, and neural networks were again less fashionable in machine learning. In the same period, computational neuroscience developed largely in parallel, building the biophysical, Bayesian and dynamical models of Chapter 13, with less direct exchange with machine learning than in the 1980s. Some exceptions bridged the two, such as reinforcement learning, where temporal-difference learning, developed by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto, was linked to dopamine signals by Wolfram Schultz, Peter Dayan and Read Montague in 1997 (Chapter 6).

2006 TO 2012: DEEP LEARNING RETURNS

In 2006 Hinton, Simon Osindero and Yee-Whye Teh showed that deep belief networks could be pretrained layer by layer with unsupervised learning, reviving interest in deep architectures. Then several things converged: large labelled datasets, especially ImageNet assembled by Fei-Fei Li's group; graphics processing units programmable for general computation; and practical techniques such as rectified linear units and dropout. In 2012 Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Hinton's convolutional network, now called AlexNet, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a top-5 error rate of about 15 percent, far ahead of the next entry at about 26 percent. Speech recognition had already been transformed by deep networks around 2009 to 2012. Deep learning rapidly became the dominant approach in AI.

The architecture that won was, at its core, Fukushima's neocognitron trained with backpropagation: a descendant of Hubel and Wiesel's cats. Chapter 8 described how, soon after, Daniel Yamins, James DiCarlo and colleagues found that the internal layers of such networks predicted responses in monkey visual cortex better than earlier models.

2013 TO 2017: REINFORCEMENT LEARNING AND ATTENTION

DeepMind, co-founded by Demis Hassabis, who had earned a PhD in cognitive neuroscience studying memory and imagination in hippocampal amnesia patients, combined deep networks with reinforcement learning. The deep Q-network, reported in Nature in 2015 by Volodymyr Mnih and colleagues, learned to play many Atari games from pixels. Its "experience replay", storing past experiences and replaying them during training, was explicitly linked by its authors to hippocampal replay (Chapter 9). AlphaGo, reported in Nature in 2016 by David Silver and colleagues, combined deep networks, reinforcement learning and tree search to defeat a top professional Go player.

In 2017 Ashish Vaswani and colleagues at Google introduced the transformer in "Attention Is All You Need", replacing recurrence with self-attention. Attention in neural networks had earlier been introduced for machine translation by Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio in 2014. Although "attention" borrows a psychological word, the transformer's mechanism, content-based weighted retrieval of values by key-query similarity, is closer mathematically to associative memory than to attention in the neuroscience sense, a point made by later work linking it to Hopfield networks (Chapter 9) and to hippocampal models.

2018 TO TODAY: SCALE

In 2018 the ACM Turing Award was given to Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun for their work on deep learning. In 2024 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks", and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was shared by Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, and David Baker, for computational protein design. The physics prize recognised work whose roots, as this chapter shows, go back to models of neurons.

Large language models, trained by self-supervised next-token prediction on enormous text corpora and then refined with methods including reinforcement learning from human feedback, became the most visible form of AI from the early 2020s. They contain no explicit models of neurons beyond the original abstraction: units computing weighted sums followed by nonlinearities.

WHAT THE HISTORY SHOWS

Three observations summarise the shared history.

First, the founding abstractions came from neuroscience: the threshold neuron, the synaptic weight, learning by changing connections, local receptive fields and hierarchical feature detection, replay, and reward prediction errors. Each has a direct line to a chapter of this book.

Second, the methods that made those abstractions work at scale came largely from mathematics, statistics, optimisation and hardware: gradient descent, backpropagation, regularisation, GPUs. Neuroscience did not provide backpropagation and for decades argued it was implausible.

Third, the relationship oscillates. In the 1940s and 1980s, the fields were closely intertwined; in the 1970s and 1990s they drifted apart; since the 2010s they have come back together, but with the arrow often pointing in the reverse direction, with deep networks serving as models of the brain and as tools for analysing neural data.

CONNECTIONS TO THE REST OF THIS BOOK

For quick reference, here is how the main AI ideas map onto earlier chapters:

Artificial neuron and threshold: McCulloch-Pitts, 04_03; the f-I curve and ReLU, 13_02.
Learning rules: Hebb, LTP and STDP, 07_01 and 07_02; Hebb versus backprop, 07_03.
Convolutional networks: retina and Hubel-Wiesel, 08_01 and 08_02; CNNs and the ventral stream, 08_03.
Memory and attention: hippocampus and H.M., 09_01; replay and consolidation, 09_02; machine memory and transformers, 09_04.
Reinforcement learning: dopamine and reward prediction error, 06_04.
Continual learning: plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, 11_03.
Generative and predictive models: 13_03.
Hardware: neuromorphic engineering, 13_04.

SUMMARY

From McCulloch and Pitts to transformers, the history of neural network AI is entangled with neuroscience. Neuroscience provided the founding metaphors and several key architectures; machine learning provided the methods that made them work; and today each field uses the other as a source of models and tools. The next section asks what each can still learn from the other.
